run-failure-patterns.1c86c8f315b4b3db27e1ecf288d824d521fe44bf:
schemaVersion: 1
name: run-failure-patterns
description: Weekly mining of this workspace's run evidence for recurring failures that nobody has filed
enabled: false
schedule:
  cron: 20 7 * * 1
template:
  title: Mine recurring run failures
  description: |-
    Mine this workspace's own run evidence for recurring failure patterns that
    are not yet tracked. The durable output is one friction record or proposed
    task per untracked pattern plus the recorded scan cursor; the execution
    summary is the audit trail. Narrative-only output does not count as delivery.

    ## Rules and command surfaces

    - Read-only against run state. Never retry, resume, cancel, or edit a run,
      and never change the status of a task a run touched. Read runs only with
      `orbit run history --limit <n> --json`, `orbit run show <run-id> --json`,
      `orbit run logs <run-id>`, and `orbit run events <run-id>`; do not read or
      edit the Orbit database or state files directly.
    - Use the registered Orbit tool surface for records. Find the newest completed
      prior instance with
      `orbit tool run orbit.task.list --input '{"status":["done"],"type":"chore","tag":["run-failure-patterns","no-diff-expected"],"limit":1,"model":"<agent-family>"}'`
      (tag filters use AND semantics) and read its cursor artifact with
      `orbit tool run orbit.task.artifact.get --input '{"id":"<id>","path":"run-failure-cursor.json","model":"<agent-family>"}'`.
      Search existing coverage with
      `orbit tool run orbit.search --input '{"query":"<one distinctive token>","kind":"all","all":true,"model":"<agent-family>"}'`
      and inspect a candidate with
      `orbit tool run orbit.task.show --input '{"id":"<id>","model":"<agent-family>"}'`.
      Lexical search matches one case-insensitive substring: pass a single
      distinctive token (an error code, step name, or tool name), never a
      multi-word phrase, and do not treat a 0-hit multi-word query as proof that
      nothing covers the pattern.
    - File a pattern with
      `orbit tool run orbit.friction.add --input '{"title":"<surface and failure>","body":"<markdown>","tags":["automation"],"during_task":"<this task ID>","model":"<agent-family>"}'`,
      or, only when the fix is clear, propose a task (tool-created tasks start
      `proposed`) with
      `orbit tool run orbit.task.add --input '{"title":"<title>","description":"<markdown>","acceptance_criteria":["<observable outcome>"],"complexity":"medium","tags":["run-failure-patterns"],"type":"bug","workspace":"<current workspace path>","model":"<agent-family>"}'`.
      Do not use direct lifecycle CLI subcommands; they skip agent provenance.
    - Fail open. A window with no new untracked pattern is a successful no-op. Do
      not invent work to justify the run.

    ## Determine the scan window

    Run the prior-instance query above. When it returns a task, read its
    `run-failure-cursor.json` artifact; its `cursor` is the RFC 3339 upper bound
    that instance scanned through, and this scan starts strictly after it. A
    selected instance without a readable cursor artifact is an error to report,
    not a first run: fall back to the cursor recorded in its execution summary,
    and fail the task if neither exists. Only when no prior instance exists, start
    the window seven days before now. The window ends at the moment this scan
    starts; record that timestamp before reading any run.

    The window contains every run whose `finished_at` falls inside it. Page
    `orbit run history --limit <n> --json` (newest first by creation) by raising
    `<n>` until the oldest returned run was created at least seven days before
    the window start, so long-running runs that finished inside the window are
    included. Runs still `pending` or `running` at scan start belong to the
    window in which they finish.

    ## Collect failure evidence

    From the window, collect:

    1. Runs whose state is `failed` or `interrupted`, and `cancelled` runs that
       recorded an error message.
    2. Step failure records: every non-success, non-skipped entry in a run's
       `steps` list, including failed steps inside runs that later succeeded
       after a retry or a recovery activity such as `step_failure_recovery`.
       Use `orbit run show <run-id> --json` for the step detail.
    3. Worker log evidence for those runs from `orbit run logs <run-id>` (and
       `--step <step-id>` for one step), read only as far as needed to name the
       error.

    ## Cluster by normalized signature

    Normalize each failure to a signature of error class, failing step, and
    tool: the error class is the stable code or leading error kind (for example
    an `error.code=` value, an HTTP status, or the failing guard name); the
    failing step is the step or deterministic action named in the error; the
    tool is the provider CLI, Orbit tool, or command that raised it. Strip run
    ids, task ids, timestamps, paths, SHAs, and counts before comparing, and
    group by the signature with the job ID as context.

    A cluster is a pattern only when it has **at least 3 occurrences across at
    least 2 distinct runs** in the window. One-offs and single-run retry loops
    below that threshold are not filed; count them in the summary only.

    ## Check coverage before filing

    For each pattern, search open and closed tasks and frictions with one
    distinctive token at a time from its signature (the error code, the step
    name, the tool name), and inspect every plausible hit. A pattern is already
    tracked when an open task or open friction describes the same underlying
    failure, or a done task does and no occurrence postdates its completion;
    record the `<signature> -> <id>` mapping and do not file. Occurrences after
    a done fix are a regression: file them as a new pattern that names the done
    task. Never file duplicates, including two records for one pattern in the
    same scan.

    ## File untracked patterns

    File exactly one record per untracked pattern: a friction by default, or a
    proposed task when the evidence makes the fix clear. The body states the
    normalized signature, occurrence count, distinct run count, first and last
    seen timestamps, up to three representative run ids, the affected job IDs,
    and one short excerpt of the error.

    Excerpts must be redacted. Quote at most a few lines, and replace tokens,
    credentials, authorization headers, cookies, email addresses, and home or
    user paths with placeholders before writing. Put excerpts only in text sent
    through `orbit.friction.add` or `orbit.task.add`, which also apply Orbit's
    write-time redaction; when the response reports `redactions_applied: true`,
    read the record back and confirm no secret-bearing context survived. Never
    attach raw logs as artifacts or copy them into other files.

    ## Record the cursor

    Always record the window bounds and the new cursor (the scan start
    timestamp) in the persisted execution summary, with runs scanned, failures
    collected, patterns found, filed ids, and already-tracked mappings. Write
    `{"schema_version":1,"cursor":"<RFC 3339 scan start>","runs_scanned":<count>}`
    to `.orbit/tmp/run-failure-cursor.json` (`$ORBIT_SCRATCH_DIR`) and attach it with
    `orbit tool run orbit.task.artifact.put --input '{"id":"<this task ID>","source_path":".orbit/tmp/run-failure-cursor.json","path":"run-failure-cursor.json","model":"<agent-family>"}'`.
    Write it on every completed scan, including an empty window.
  acceptance_criteria:
  - The scan window started at the previous completed instance's recorded cursor, or seven days before the scan on the first run, and ended at the recorded scan start.
  - Failures were clustered by normalized signature, and only clusters with at least 3 occurrences across at least 2 distinct runs were treated as patterns.
  - Open and closed tasks and frictions were searched for every pattern before filing, and no duplicate record was filed.
  - Every filed record carries the signature, occurrence count, first and last seen, representative run ids, and a redacted excerpt.
  - No run was retried, resumed, cancelled, or edited, and no run state was mutated.
  - The execution summary reports runs scanned, patterns found, filed versus already-tracked ids, and the window bounds, and the new cursor is attached as `run-failure-cursor.json`.
  - A window with no new untracked pattern succeeds as a no-op.
  task_type: chore
  tags:
  - run-failure-patterns
  - no-diff-expected
  priority: medium
  complexity: medium
  # The portable system lane is seeded per machine and compatibility-aliased
  # for configs written before that crew existed.

name: run-failure-patterns
description: Weekly mining of this workspace's run evidence for recurring failures that nobody has filed
enabled: false
schedule:
  cron: 20 7 * * 1
template:
  title: Mine recurring run failures
  description: |-
    Mine this workspace's own run evidence for recurring failure patterns that
    are not yet tracked. The durable output is one friction record or proposed
    task per untracked pattern plus the recorded scan cursor; the execution
    summary is the audit trail. Narrative-only output does not count as delivery.

    ## Rules and command surfaces

    - Read-only against run state. Never retry, resume, cancel, or edit a run,
      and never change the status of a task a run touched. Read runs only with
      `orbit run history --limit <n> --no-reconcile --json`,
      `orbit run show <run-id> --no-reconcile --json`,
      `orbit run logs <run-id> --no-reconcile`, and
      `orbit run events <run-id> --no-reconcile`; do not read or edit the Orbit
      database or state files directly. Never drop `--no-reconcile`: without it
      these reads finalize an orphaned `pending` or `running` run as
      `interrupted` and release its task reservations.
    - Use the registered Orbit tool surface for records. Find the newest completed
      prior instance with
      `orbit tool run orbit.task.list --input '{"status":["done"],"type":"chore","tag":["run-failure-patterns","no-diff-expected"],"limit":1,"model":"<agent-family>"}'`
      (tag filters use AND semantics) and read its cursor artifact with
      `orbit tool run orbit.task.artifact.get --input '{"id":"<id>","path":"run-failure-cursor.json","model":"<agent-family>"}'`.
      Search existing coverage with
      `orbit tool run orbit.search --input '{"query":"<one distinctive token>","kind":"all","all":true,"model":"<agent-family>"}'`
      and inspect a candidate with
      `orbit tool run orbit.task.show --input '{"id":"<id>","model":"<agent-family>"}'`.
      Lexical search matches one case-insensitive substring: pass a single
      distinctive token (an error code, step name, or tool name), never a
      multi-word phrase, and do not treat a 0-hit multi-word query as proof that
      nothing covers the pattern.
    - File a pattern with
      `orbit tool run orbit.friction.add --input '{"title":"<surface and failure>","body":"<markdown>","tags":["automation"],"during_task":"<this task ID>","model":"<agent-family>"}'`,
      or, only when the fix is clear, propose a task (tool-created tasks start
      `proposed`) with
      `orbit tool run orbit.task.add --input '{"title":"<title>","description":"<markdown>","acceptance_criteria":["<observable outcome>"],"complexity":"medium","tags":["run-failure-patterns"],"type":"bug","workspace":"<current workspace path>","model":"<agent-family>"}'`.
      Do not use direct lifecycle CLI subcommands; they skip agent provenance.
    - Fail open. A window with no new untracked pattern is a successful no-op. Do
      not invent work to justify the run.

    ## Determine the scan window

    Run the prior-instance query above. When it returns a task, read its
    `run-failure-cursor.json` artifact; its `cursor` is the RFC 3339 upper bound
    that instance scanned through, and this scan starts strictly after it. A
    selected instance without a readable cursor artifact is an error to report,
    not a first run: fall back to the cursor recorded in its execution summary,
    and fail the task if neither exists. Only when no prior instance exists, start
    the window seven days before now. The window ends at the moment this scan
    starts; record that timestamp before reading any run.

    The window contains every run whose `finished_at` falls inside it. Page
    `orbit run history --limit <n> --no-reconcile --json` (newest first by
    creation) by raising `<n>` until the oldest returned run was created at
    least seven days before the window start, so long-running runs that
    finished inside the window are included. Runs still `pending` or `running` at scan start belong to the
    window in which they finish.

    ## Collect failure evidence

    From the window, collect:

    1. Runs whose state is `failed` or `interrupted`, and `cancelled` runs that
       recorded an error message.
    2. Step failure records: every non-success, non-skipped entry in a run's
       `steps` list, including failed steps inside runs that later succeeded
       after a retry or a recovery activity such as `step_failure_recovery`.
       Use `orbit run show <run-id> --no-reconcile --json` for the step detail.
    3. Worker log evidence for those runs from
       `orbit run logs <run-id> --no-reconcile` (and `--step <step-id>` for one
       step), read only as far as needed to name the error.

    ## Cluster by normalized signature

    Normalize each failure to a signature of error class, failing step, and
    tool: the error class is the stable code or leading error kind (for example
    an `error.code=` value, an HTTP status, or the failing guard name); the
    failing step is the step or deterministic action named in the error; the
    tool is the provider CLI, Orbit tool, or command that raised it. Strip run
    ids, task ids, timestamps, paths, SHAs, and counts before comparing, and
    group by the signature with the job ID as context.

    A cluster is a pattern only when it has **at least 3 occurrences across at
    least 2 distinct runs** in the window. One-offs and single-run retry loops
    below that threshold are not filed; count them in the summary only.

    ## Check coverage before filing

    For each pattern, search open and closed tasks and frictions with one
    distinctive token at a time from its signature (the error code, the step
    name, the tool name), and inspect every plausible hit. A pattern is already
    tracked when an open task or open friction describes the same underlying
    failure, or a done task does and no occurrence postdates its completion;
    record the `<signature> -> <id>` mapping and do not file. Occurrences after
    a done fix are a regression: file them as a new pattern that names the done
    task. Never file duplicates, including two records for one pattern in the
    same scan.

    ## File untracked patterns

    File exactly one record per untracked pattern: a friction by default, or a
    proposed task when the evidence makes the fix clear. The body states the
    normalized signature, occurrence count, distinct run count, first and last
    seen timestamps, up to three representative run ids, the affected job IDs,
    and one short excerpt of the error.

    Excerpts must be redacted. Quote at most a few lines, and replace tokens,
    credentials, authorization headers, cookies, email addresses, and home or
    user paths with placeholders before writing. Put excerpts only in text sent
    through `orbit.friction.add` or `orbit.task.add`, which also apply Orbit's
    write-time redaction; when the response reports `redactions_applied: true`,
    read the record back and confirm no secret-bearing context survived. Never
    attach raw logs as artifacts or copy them into other files.

    ## Record the cursor

    Always record the window bounds and the new cursor (the scan start
    timestamp) in the persisted execution summary, with runs scanned, failures
    collected, patterns found, filed ids, and already-tracked mappings. Write
    `{"schema_version":1,"cursor":"<RFC 3339 scan start>","runs_scanned":<count>}`
    to `.orbit/tmp/run-failure-cursor.json` (`$ORBIT_SCRATCH_DIR`) and attach it with
    `orbit tool run orbit.task.artifact.put --input '{"id":"<this task ID>","source_path":".orbit/tmp/run-failure-cursor.json","path":"run-failure-cursor.json","model":"<agent-family>"}'`.
    Write it on every completed scan, including an empty window.
  acceptance_criteria:
  - The scan window started at the previous completed instance's recorded cursor, or seven days before the scan on the first run, and ended at the recorded scan start.
  - Failures were clustered by normalized signature, and only clusters with at least 3 occurrences across at least 2 distinct runs were treated as patterns.
  - Open and closed tasks and frictions were searched for every pattern before filing, and no duplicate record was filed.
  - Every filed record carries the signature, occurrence count, first and last seen, representative run ids, and a redacted excerpt.
  - No run was retried, resumed, cancelled, or edited, and no run state was mutated.
  - The execution summary reports runs scanned, patterns found, filed versus already-tracked ids, and the window bounds, and the new cursor is attached as `run-failure-cursor.json`.
  - A window with no new untracked pattern succeeds as a no-op.
  task_type: chore
  tags:
  - run-failure-patterns
  - no-diff-expected
  priority: medium
  complexity: medium
  # The portable system lane is seeded per machine and compatibility-aliased
  # for configs written before that crew existed.
  crew: system
  status: backlog

      drop `--no-reconcile`: without it the run reads finalize an orphaned
      `pending` or `running` run as `interrupted` and release its task
      reservations, and the settlement read recovers an interrupted
      coordination commit.
    - Use the registered Orbit tool surface for records. Find the newest completed
      prior instance with
      `orbit tool run orbit.task.list --input '{"status":["done"],"type":"chore","tag":["run-failure-patterns","no-diff-expected"],"limit":1,"model":"<agent-family>"}'`
      (tag filters use AND semantics) and read its cursor artifact with
      `orbit tool run orbit.task.artifact.get --input '{"id":"<id>","path":"run-failure-cursor.json","model":"<agent-family>"}'`.
      Search existing coverage with
      `orbit tool run orbit.search --input '{"query":"<one distinctive token>","kind":"all","all":true,"model":"<agent-family>"}'`
      and inspect a candidate with
      `orbit tool run orbit.task.show --input '{"id":"<id>","model":"<agent-family>"}'`.
      Lexical search matches one case-insensitive substring: pass a single
      distinctive token (an error code, step name, or tool name), never a
      multi-word phrase, and do not treat a 0-hit multi-word query as proof that
      nothing covers the pattern.
    - Before filing a fix task, read the installed `orbit` skill's
      task-authoring reference (`references/task-authoring.md`) and follow it
      for task shape. File each fix task (tool-created tasks start `proposed`)
      with
      `orbit tool run orbit.task.add --input '{"title":"<surface and failure>","description":"<markdown>","acceptance_criteria":["<observable outcome>"],"context_files":["file:<verified path>"],"complexity":"<assessed>","tags":["run-failure-patterns","no-auto-approve"],"type":"bug","workspace":"<current workspace path>","model":"<agent-family>"}'`.
      Add `"crew":"opus"` when the assessed complexity is `hard` or `xhard`.
      The `no-auto-approve` tag keeps the task `proposed` for human approval:
      an `--approve-proposed` drain never promotes it. File a friction instead
      only when the evidence cannot establish a cause, with
      `orbit tool run orbit.friction.add --input '{"title":"<surface and failure>","body":"<markdown>","tags":["automation","run-failure-patterns"],"during_task":"<this task ID>","model":"<agent-family>"}'`.
      Never file both for one pattern: friction curation turns frictions into
      tasks, so a friction beside a fix task duplicates the work. Do not use
      direct lifecycle CLI subcommands; they skip agent provenance.
    - Fail open. A window with no new untracked pattern is a successful no-op. Do
      not invent work to justify the run.

    ## Determine the scan window

    Run the prior-instance query above. When it returns a task, read its
    `run-failure-cursor.json` artifact; its `cursor` is the RFC 3339 upper bound
    that instance scanned through, and this scan starts strictly after it. A
    selected instance without a readable cursor artifact is an error to report,
    not a first run: fall back to the cursor recorded in its execution summary,
    and fail the task if neither exists. Only when no prior instance exists, start
    the window seven days before now. The window ends at the moment this scan
    starts; record that timestamp before reading any run.

    The window contains every run whose `finished_at` falls inside it. Page
    `orbit run history --limit <n> --no-reconcile --json` (newest first by
    creation) by raising `<n>` until the oldest returned run was created at
    least seven days before the window start, so long-running runs that
    finished inside the window are included. Runs still `pending` or `running` at scan start belong to the
    window in which they finish.

    ## Collect failure evidence

    From the window, collect:

    1. Runs whose state is `failed` or `interrupted`, and `cancelled` runs that
       recorded an error message.
    2. Step failure records: every non-success, non-skipped entry in a run's
       `steps` list, including failed steps inside runs that later succeeded
       after a retry or a recovery activity such as `step_failure_recovery`.
       Use `orbit run show <run-id> --no-reconcile --json` for the step detail.
    3. Worker log evidence for those runs from
       `orbit run logs <run-id> --no-reconcile` (and `--step <step-id>` for one
       step), read only as far as needed to name the error.
    4. Follower leaf failures. A claimed leaf runs on a follower host, so this
       host's run history never lists it; its owner keeps the failure or
       release settlement the leaf sent. Each entry of
       `orbit run settlements --since <window start> --no-reconcile --json`
       whose `settled_at` falls in the window is one occurrence in one run
       (its `leaf_run_id`) on host `machine_name` or `machine_id`. Its
       `evidence` names the class (`provider_unavailable`, `baseline_red`,
       `forge_unavailable`, `final_recovery`, `failure`, `summary`),
       `failure_class` the typed failure, `failed_step_id` the step, and
       `reason` the leaf's own diagnostic. An `unrecorded` entry settled
       before the owner kept settlements: take its reason from the task's
       history `note` or comment at `settled_at` through `orbit.task.show`.
       An `evidence_hold` release, and an `operator_cancel` failure class,
       are designed outcomes, not failures. A leaf run that also appears in
       this host's run history is one occurrence, not two. When the read
       refuses because a coordination commit is pending, record that in the
       summary and continue without follower evidence. In a follower's
       replica checkout the list is empty; leave its claimed leaves (jobs
       `task_claimed_pr_pipeline` and `task_claimed_local_pipeline`) to the
       owner's scan, which counts them from these settlements.

    ## Fold cascades by recorded cause

    A parent pipeline whose child fails also fails, in
    `pipeline_success_guard`. Fold parents by the recorded cause, never by
    judgment or by matching error text: read `root_cause` from
    `orbit run show <run-id> --no-reconcile --json` for every failed run.
    When `root_cause.run_id` names another run, the run is an echo of that
    run: count the occurrence once, at the root cause. When the root cause is
    a `pipeline_success_guard` failure, read its run's
    `pipeline_state.child_dispatches[].child_run_id` and their states: a
    `held` child is a designed hold (review evidence, a red base, a forge
    outage), so neither that run nor any parent folded into it is a failure.
    Report the fold count and the held-chain count in the summary.

    ## Cluster by normalized signature

    Normalize each failure to a signature of error class, failing step, and
    tool: the error class is the stable code or leading error kind (for example
    an `error.code=` value, an HTTP status, the failing guard name, or a
    settlement's `evidence` and `failure_class`); the failing step is the step
    or deterministic action named in the error; the tool is the provider CLI,
    Orbit tool, or command that raised it. Strip run ids, task ids, timestamps,
    paths, SHAs, host names, and counts before comparing, and group by the
    signature with the job ID and host as context. One pattern seen on this
    host and on a follower is one pattern.

    Split review refusals. A `review_gate_settle` or `review` refusal also
    carries an escalation category, read from the refusal's error message
    (`review_gate_blocked: verdict <verdict> (<escalation>)`, a
    `[baseline_red]` marker, or `review_timeout_incomplete`; a follower
    settlement's `reason`) and, for the
    task's latest attempt, from the stored review evidence read with
    `orbit.task.artifact.get`: `review-gate.json` (`verdict`, `escalation`)
    and `review-report.json` (`verdict`, `escalation`, `external_evidence`,
    and each `validation[]` record's `outcome` and `role`). Each category is a
    pattern by itself:

    - `base_red`: a `[baseline_red]` refusal, or an escalation saying a
      required check fails on the base, is pre-existing, or needs a green base.
    - `external_evidence`: a non-empty `external_evidence`, or an escalation
      asking for evidence the reviewer's host cannot produce: a native OS
      (`native_os`), a hosted CI result (`hosted_ci`), or CodeQL (`codeql`).
    - `report_revision`: the gate refused the reviewer's report or its
      revisions, such as `validation_incomplete` for a required check an
      earlier revision recorded and the final one omits, a superseded attempt
      with no replacing pass, or a report or certificate mismatch.
    - `scope_or_criteria`: a `reject` whose escalation says the task's scope,
      acceptance criteria or approach must change.
    - `timeout`: the reviewer exceeded its wall clock or review budget.
    - `other`: anything else.

    A cluster is a pattern when it has **at least 3 occurrences across at
    least 2 distinct runs** in the window. Below that threshold, a single
    occurrence is still a pattern when all of these hold:

    - it came from a deterministic Orbit action (a step such as `git_push`,
      `git_commit`, `pr_open`, `pr_complete` or a guard) or a tool limit (a
      timeout clamp, a size cap), not a provider (authentication, capacity,
      rate limit), capacity or network error (DNS, TLS, status 000, a
      connection reset), which stay counted only;
    - it blocked a task (the task is `blocked`, or its claim failed) or
      needed an operator rerun or resume;
    - the code verification below shows it would recur under the same
      conditions.

    Count every other one-off and single-run retry loop in the summary only.

    ## Check coverage before filing

    For each pattern, search open and closed tasks and frictions with one
    distinctive token at a time from its signature (the error code, the step
    name, the tool name, the escalation category), and inspect every plausible
    hit. A pattern is already tracked when an open task (including a
    `proposed` one) or open friction describes the same underlying failure, a
    done task does and no occurrence postdates its completion, or a rejected
    task's rationale decided the same failure is not to be fixed; record the
    `<signature> -> <id>` mapping and do not file. Occurrences after a done fix
    are a regression: file them as a new pattern that names the done task.
    Never file duplicates, including two records for one pattern in the same
    scan.

    ## Verify the mechanism in code

    For every untracked pattern, find the mechanism in this checkout, which
    is at the workspace's current integration base; record
    `git rev-parse HEAD`. Name the file and function that raise or permit the
    failure, and quote the guard, comment or constant that explains it (a
    few lines). A pattern whose cause the evidence and code cannot establish
    is filed as a friction, not a task.

    ## File untracked patterns

    File exactly one record per untracked pattern: a proposed fix task, or a
    friction when no cause could be established. The body carries:

    - the problem, in a sentence or two;
    - an evidence table: normalized signature, occurrence count, distinct
      run count, hosts, first and last seen timestamps, up to three
      representative run ids, the affected job IDs, and one short redacted
      excerpt;
    - the verified mechanism: file, function, quoted guard and commit;
    - for a task, the proposed change; then observable acceptance criteria,
      `context_files` naming the verified files, and an assessed complexity.

    Excerpts must be redacted. Quote at most a few lines, and replace tokens,
    credentials, authorization headers, cookies, email addresses, and home or
    user paths with placeholders before writing. Put excerpts only in text sent
    through `orbit.friction.add` or `orbit.task.add`, which also apply Orbit's
    write-time redaction; when the response reports `redactions_applied: true`,
    read the record back and confirm no secret-bearing context survived. Never
    attach raw logs as artifacts or copy them into other files.

    ## Record the cursor

    Always record the window bounds and the new cursor (the scan start
    timestamp) in the persisted execution summary, with runs scanned,
    follower settlements read, failures collected, the fold and held-chain
    counts, patterns found, filed ids, already-tracked mappings, and the
    one-offs counted but not filed. Write
    `{"schema_version":1,"cursor":"<RFC 3339 scan start>","runs_scanned":<count>}`
    to `.orbit/tmp/run-failure-cursor.json` (`$ORBIT_SCRATCH_DIR`) and attach it with
    `orbit tool run orbit.task.artifact.put --input '{"id":"<this task ID>","source_path":".orbit/tmp/run-failure-cursor.json","path":"run-failure-cursor.json","model":"<agent-family>"}'`.
    `orbit tool show <tool.name>` prints the tool's schema.
    Write it on every completed scan, including an empty window.
  acceptance_criteria:
  - The scan window started at the previous completed instance's recorded cursor, or seven days before the scan on the first run, and ended at the recorded scan start.
  - Follower leaf settlements from `orbit run settlements --no-reconcile` were counted with this host's runs, and failed parents were folded by their recorded `root_cause`, with a held child's parents not counted as failures.
  - Failures were clustered by normalized signature, with review refusals split by escalation category, and only clusters with at least 3 occurrences across at least 2 distinct runs, or a blocking deterministic Orbit-action or tool-limit one-off, were treated as patterns.
  - Open and closed tasks and frictions were searched for every pattern before filing, and no duplicate record was filed.
  - Every untracked pattern's mechanism was verified in code, and it was filed as one proposed fix task tagged `run-failure-patterns` and `no-auto-approve`, or as a friction only when no cause could be established, never both.
  - Every filed record carries the signature, occurrence count, first and last seen, representative run ids, and a redacted excerpt.
  - No run was retried, resumed, cancelled, or edited, and no run state was mutated.
  - The execution summary reports runs scanned, patterns found, filed versus already-tracked ids, and the window bounds, and the new cursor is attached as `run-failure-cursor.json`.
  - A window with no new untracked pattern succeeds as a no-op.
  task_type: chore
  tags:
  - run-failure-patterns
  - no-diff-expected
  required_tools:
  - orbit.friction.add
  - orbit.search
  - orbit.task.add
  - orbit.task.artifact.get
  - orbit.task.artifact.put
  - orbit.task.list
  - orbit.task.show
  priority: medium
  complexity: medium
  # The portable system lane is seeded per machine and compatibility-aliased
  # for configs written before that crew existed.
  crew: system
  status: backlog

schemaVersion: 1
name: security-review
description: Weekly evidence-backed review of application, dependency, secret-handling, and configuration risks
enabled: false
schedule:
  cron: 0 8 * * 1
template:
  title: Review workspace security
  description: |-
    Perform a weekly security review of this workspace. The durable output is filed Orbit tasks for every actionable finding; the execution summary is only an audit trail. Narrative-only output does not count as delivery.

    ## Rules and command surfaces

    - Use the registered Orbit tool surface. Search coverage with `orbit tool run orbit.search --input '{"query":"<distinctive symptom, component, or CVE terms>","kind":"task","all":true,"model":"<agent-family>"}'`. List open security-review work with `orbit tool run orbit.task.list --input '{"status":["backlog","in-progress","proposed","blocked"],"tag":"security-review","model":"<agent-family>"}'`. Inspect a candidate with `orbit tool run orbit.task.show --input '{"id":"<id>","model":"<agent-family>"}'`. File a finding with `orbit tool run orbit.task.add --input '{"title":"<title>","description":"<markdown>","acceptance_criteria":["<observable outcome>"],"complexity":"medium","tags":["security-review"],"priority":"<low|medium|high|critical>","type":"bug","workspace":"<current workspace path>","model":"<agent-family>"}'`. Do not use direct lifecycle CLI subcommands; they skip agent provenance.
    - Before filing anything, check for duplicate open tasks covering the same underlying issue, including open tasks tagged `security-review`. Skip duplicates. If an open or done task already covers the finding, record the `<finding> -> <task-id>` mapping in the execution summary instead of filing another copy.
    - Every actionable finding must be a durable, deduplicated Orbit task with reproducible evidence and severity/impact. Include the exact file paths, commands, dependency names and versions, configuration keys, or secret-handling locations that demonstrate the issue, plus a severity rating and an impact statement. Do not leave findings in narrative-only output.
    - Fail open. A clean review with no findings is a successful no-op. Do not invent work to justify the run.

    ## Review scope

    Review only what applies to this workspace. Cite evidence from the current tree, lockfiles, configuration, and tests. Do not guess.

    1. Application code. Inspect authentication, authorization, input validation, injection, unsafe deserialization, SSRF, path traversal, and other applicable code-level risks in the paths this workspace actually ships.
    2. Dependencies. Inspect manifests and lockfiles for known-vulnerable, unpinned, abandoned, or unexpectedly added packages. Record the package, version, and advisory source.
    3. Secret handling. Inspect how credentials, tokens, keys, and other secrets are stored, loaded, logged, and excluded from version control. Flag hardcoded secrets, secrets in logs, world-readable secret files, and missing ignore rules.
    4. Configuration. Inspect service, sandbox, CI, and deployment configuration for overly permissive access, debug or insecure defaults on production paths, and missing hardening this workspace is expected to have.

    ## Pass

    1. Snapshot existing open `security-review` tasks and search for overlapping coverage of each candidate finding.
    2. Review the four areas above and collect evidence-backed findings only.
    3. For each actionable, non-duplicate finding, file exactly one Orbit task through `orbit tool run orbit.task.add` with reproduction evidence, severity, and impact. Read it back with `orbit tool run orbit.task.show` before recording it as delivered.
    4. If there are no findings, persist an execution summary that the review was clean and succeed. Do not file filler tasks.
  acceptance_criteria:
  - Applicable application code, dependencies, secret handling, and configuration were reviewed with evidence from the current workspace.
  - Existing open tasks were searched and duplicate findings were not filed.
  - Every actionable finding was filed as a durable Orbit task with reproducible evidence, severity, and impact; narrative-only output is not delivery.
  - A clean review with no findings succeeds as a no-op.
  task_type: chore
  tags:
  - security-review
  - no-diff-expected
  priority: medium
  complexity: hard
  # The portable system lane is seeded per machine and compatibility-aliased
  # for configs written before that crew existed.
  crew: system
  status: backlog
dedupe: skip_if_open

updated_by: system
